reading.intro: Saturday, ten to eight in the evening. Maya has an empty fridge and a long list. Lena comes along. The supermarket closes at eight, and tomorrow is Sunday.
reading.photos[0].caption: Einkaufswagen: Ein Euro rein, dann fährt der Wagen.
reading.photos[1].caption: Auf dem Wochenmarkt: Radieschen, ein Bund, 1 Euro.
reading.en: Maya: Lena, I need a cart. But this cart is broken. · Lena: It isn't broken. It needs a euro. · Maya: I don't have a euro. I only have a card. · Lena: Here's a euro. What do you need? · Maya: Milk, eggs, a lettuce, a kilo of apples and a bottle of wine. · Lena: Do you have a bag? · Maya: No, I have no bag. · Lena: Then we'll take a paper bag. Quick! It's five to eight! · At the till. · Verkäuferin: Eighteen euros forty. Would you like the receipt? · Maya: Yes, please. – Oh no! The coffee! I have no coffee! · Lena: No problem. You'll buy it tomorrow. · Verkäuferin: Tomorrow is Sunday. On Sunday everything is closed. · Maya: Everything? No coffee until Monday? · Verkäuferin: A kiosk is open at the station. The coffee there isn't cheap. · Lena: And Maya … my euro is still in the cart.
reading.fact: Shops are closed on Sundays almost everywhere in Germany. Bakeries open for a few hours, stations and petrol stations stay open, and that is why half the town meets at the station on a Sunday, buying milk.
reading.tasks[1].instruction: Write it with the amount, as in the text.
document.caption: Ein Kassenbon aus Köln: Was hat der Kunde gekauft?
document.intro: A real receipt from a pet shop in Cologne. *Summe* is the total, *Bar* is cash, *Rückgeld* is your change. The rest you can ignore, as everyone does.
document.fact: Every shop in Germany must offer you a receipt, even for one roll. That is why bakers ask *Bon?* and why so many end up in the bin by the door.
document.tasks[0].instruction: Find it on the receipt and write the amount.
